He walked with a stiff gait. He had worsening difficulties in academic achievement and behavioral disorders. IQ was normal, but a long-term memory deficit was apparent. Results of standard studies of blood and cerebral fluid were normal. Islet cells and GAD antibodies were present at high titers. GAD antibodies reacted as reported in SPS.4 A search for a malignancy was negative. Histologic findings in muscle and nerve tissue specimens were normal. Electromyography (EMG) revealed continuous motor unit potentials in paraspinal muscles and limbs, which varied with sensory stimuli.

extractions.quote: Stiff-person syndrome (SPS) is a rare autoimmune disorder characterized by progressive stiffness of the paraspinal and lower limb musculature and intermittent painful spasms.1 SPS mostly affects adults, and cases in children have been rare.2,3 SPS may be associated with type 1 diabetes, and with antibodies to glutamate decarboxylase (GAD).4 Cerebral aspects on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are variable, and limbic lesions have been described.1,5 Several therapies have been used with variable success.6 Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) has been ef���cacious in adults.7-9 A 12-year-old boy presented with a 3-year history of well-controlled type 1 diabetes. A stiffness of the distal right leg had appeared a few months before, which extended to all limbs and to abdominal, intercostal, and paraspinal muscles with lumbar hyperlordosis. He walked with a stiff gait. He had worsening difficulties in academic achievement and behavioral disorders. IQ was normal, but a long-term memory deficit was apparent. Results of standard studies of blood and cerebral ���uid were normal. Islet cells and GAD antibodies were present at high titers. GAD antibodies reacted as reported in SPS.4 A search for a malignancy was negative. Histologic ���ndings in muscle and nerve tissue specimens were normal. Electromyography (EMG) revealed continuous motor unit potentials in paraspinal muscles and limbs, which varied with sensory stimuli. Cerebral MRI revealed an area of bright signal on FLAIR sequences located in the right hippocampal region. The patient’s symptoms were poorly relieved by baclofen, diazepam, and vigabatrin. He was given 6 courses of IVIG (Tegeline, 1 g/kg/d for 3 days) 1 month apart, and his progress was assessed monthly by means of a videotaped walking task. A progressive reduction of stiffness was noticed, starting after the second course. The intractable flexion of ankles, knees, and hips, as well as the hyperlordotic posture, was reduced. He regained the ability to easily climb stairs and to run. There was no significant memory loss, and no EMG or MRI changes were observed. At the time of this report, 6 months after the end of the IVIG therapy, the improvement is sustained.
